rationale: B wins because it is stricter about proof and beat fit, not because A is weak. B's "It has not said how often they get it wrong" turns the missing reliability data into a real enterprise IT story, while A's "pre-AI decacorns rebrand to survive" smuggles in a market narrative the fact block did not hand it. A has good bones; B has fewer places where a skeptical reporter can stick a knife.
gaps_in_A: "pre-AI decacorns rebrand to survive" invents motive and a broader press narrative. The update says valuation is down and messaging is shifting; it does not prove survival pressure.
"formally retiring the 'spreadsheet-database' identity" overstates "shifting its messaging." Retiring an identity is stronger than the supplied fact.
"An enterprise-software or private-markets reporter" blurs two beats in the first angle. Pick the money reporter or the enterprise software reporter; their editors want different stories.
"three viable shapes exist" is too generous when angle three says it is "not pitchable until Airtable can supply agent-reliability data." Useful warning, but do not call the hole a viable pitch yet.
gaps_in_B: "publicly abandoning that identity" overstates the supplied fact. The company is shifting messaging; abandonment is a sharper verb than the evidence supports.
"repositioning of a widely known product" imports outside context. Airtable may be widely known, but that was not in the update.

"Pricing is not finalized, so there is nothing to report yet" is too dismissive. No pricing story yet, fine, but missing pricing is still a product-launch credibility problem reporters will ask about.

"where agents do the work" is clean copy, but it rounds up the product claim. The facts say agents read records and take actions like status updates and email drafts, not that they take over workflows broadly.
